question: How have Apple's regulatory disclosures changed from 2023 through 2025, and what actions does management describe?

scopes.description: AAPL: fiscal years FY2023, FY2024, FY2025 (FY2023, FY2024, FY2025).

notes: Years are read as each company’s own fiscal years.

brief.title: Apple Regulatory Disclosure Evolution: FY2023–FY2025
brief.executiveSummary: Apple's regulatory risk disclosures have grown materially in specificity and scope from FY2023 through FY2025, moving from forward-looking warnings about the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) compliance deadline to reporting concrete implemented changes across the App Store, iOS, iPadOS, and Safari in both the EU and the U.S. By FY2025, disclosures added new dimensions not present in FY2023: a U.S. court order prohibiting commissions on certain purchases, the Google antitrust ruling and its potential impact on Apple's search licensing revenue, and new U.S. tariffs on imports from key manufacturing countries. Management's described actions have correspondingly shifted from anticipatory compliance planning to active, ongoing remediation and engagement with regulators.
followUpQuestions: What specific financial accruals or contingent liabilities has Apple recorded in its legal proceedings footnotes across FY2023, FY2024, and FY2025 in connection with App Store and antitrust matters?
How has Apple's Services segment revenue and gross margin trended across FY2023, FY2024, and FY2025, and do the filings attribute any changes to regulatory-driven App Store modifications?
What does Apple disclose in its FY2025 10-K regarding the specific DMA compliance plan provisions that have been challenged by the European Commission?
How does Apple describe the tax implications of the EU DMA compliance changes and the Google antitrust remedies in its uncertain tax positions disclosures across FY2023–FY2025?

investmentConsiderations.text: The progression from anticipated DMA compliance (FY2023) to implemented changes now under active Commission challenge (FY2024–FY2025) signals that Apple's App Store business model in the EU faces ongoing structural uncertainty. The DMA provides for significant fines and penalties for noncompliance, and the compliance plan may be challenged further by private litigants, creating a multi-front legal exposure that a diligence team should assess for potential revenue and margin impact.

The FY2025 disclosure of a U.S. court order prohibiting Apple from imposing any commission or fee on certain purchases, combined with named U.S. civil antitrust lawsuits alleging smartphone market monopolization, represents a material escalation in domestic legal risk to the App Store revenue model that was not present in FY2023 disclosures. Diligence teams should evaluate the potential scope of commission revenue at risk.

The Google antitrust ruling and associated court remedies, first disclosed in FY2025, introduce a specific and quantifiable risk to Apple's search licensing revenue. The filing notes that DOJ-proposed remedies could prohibit Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution, and that a reversal on appeal could result in imposition of such remedies. This is a new, named revenue risk absent from FY2023 and FY2024 filings.

The FY2025 introduction of a dedicated tariff section in the MD&A, covering new U.S. tariffs on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the EU, plus a Section 232 semiconductor investigation, signals that supply chain and cost structure risks have become a front-line regulatory concern. The filing states the ultimate impact remains uncertain and depends on several factors including additional tariffs, retaliatory measures, and the magnitude and duration of these measures.

keyFindings.title: DMA Compliance: From Deadline Warning to Implemented Changes
keyFindings.finding: In FY2023, Apple disclosed it was required to comply with the EU Digital Markets Act by March 2024 and expected to make further business changes. By FY2024 and FY2025, the filings report that Apple has implemented changes to iOS, iPadOS, the App Store, and Safari in the EU, including new business terms, alternative fee structures, alternative distribution methods, alternative payment processing, and additional developer tools and APIs. The FY2024 and FY2025 filings also note that Apple has continued to make changes to its compliance plan in response to feedback and engagement with the European Commission, and that the compliance plan has been challenged by the Commission and may be challenged further by private litigants.

keyFindings.title: U.S. App Store: New Court Order Prohibiting Commissions Added in FY2025
keyFindings.finding: FY2023 and FY2024 disclosures noted U.S. changes to how developers communicate with consumers regarding alternative purchasing mechanisms. FY2025 adds a materially new disclosure: Apple is currently subject to a court order preventing it from imposing any commission or fee on certain purchases that consumers make, a specific legal constraint absent from prior-year filings.

All three years disclose that Apple earns revenue from licensing arrangements with other companies (including Google) to offer search services, and that these arrangements are subject to government investigations and legal proceedings. FY2025 adds a specific new development: on August 5, 2024, Google was found to have violated U.S. antitrust laws, and on September 2, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ordered certain remedies. The filing notes that a reversal on appeal could result in DOJ-proposed remedies prohibiting Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution, which could materially adversely affect Apple's ability to earn revenue from such arrangements.
keyFindings.title: Google Search Licensing Risk Escalates to Named Antitrust Ruling

keyFindings.finding: FY2023 disclosed antitrust investigations in various jurisdictions and European App Store investigations in general terms. FY2024 and FY2025 filings specifically name civil antitrust lawsuits in the U.S. alleging monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for 'performance smartphones' and 'smartphones' generally in violation of U.S. antitrust laws, a more specific and escalated disclosure.
keyFindings.title: U.S. Antitrust Lawsuits Named Explicitly Starting FY2024
AI/ML Regulatory Risk Added as New Dimension in FY2024–FY2025
keyFindings.finding: FY2023 disclosures do not mention artificial intelligence or machine learning in the regulatory compliance risk context. FY2024 adds that regulatory risks and costs may increase as Apple expands the use of machine learning and artificial intelligence features and must navigate new legal, regulatory and ethical considerations. FY2025 further notes that AI features can exacerbate risks of inadvertent personal data disclosure, and that novel IP claims may be exacerbated as AI is further integrated into products and services.

keyFindings.title: FY2025 Adds Tariff Exposure as a New Regulatory/Trade Risk Category
keyFindings.finding: FY2023 and FY2024 filings reference export/import regulatory risk in general terms. FY2025 introduces a dedicated 'Tariffs and Other Measures' section in the MD&A, disclosing that beginning in the second quarter of 2025, new U.S. tariffs were announced on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the EU, among others, and that several countries have imposed or threatened reciprocal tariffs. The filing also notes a U.S. Department of Commerce investigation under Section 232 into semiconductor imports and downstream products.

evidenceGaps: No 10-Q filings are included in the excerpts; intra-year regulatory developments between annual filings are not covered.
The excerpts do not include quantified financial impact of App Store regulatory changes (e.g., revenue or commission amounts at risk) in any of the three fiscal years.

The excerpts do not include Apple's legal proceedings footnotes (typically in financial statement notes), which would provide more granular detail on specific litigation status, accruals, and settlement terms.
The excerpts do not cover the specific terms or financial magnitude of Apple's search licensing arrangements with Google or other companies.
No FY2025 10-Q filings are included, so any regulatory developments after the FY2025 10-K filing date (October 31, 2025) are not covered.

citations.section: Item 1A — Risk Factors › Legal and Regulatory Compliance Risks
citations.text: Compliance with these laws and regulations is onerous and expensive. New and changing laws and regulations can adversely affect the Company’s business by increasing the Company’s costs, limiting the Company’s ability to offer a product, service or feature to customers, imposing changes to the design of the Company’s products and services, impacting customer demand for the Company’s products and services, and requiring changes to the Company’s supply chain and its business. New and changing laws and regulations can also create uncertainty about how such laws and regulations will be interpreted and applied. These risks and costs may increase as the Company’s products and services are introduced into specialized applications, including health and financial services. The Company has implemented policies and procedures designed to ensure compliance with applicable laws and regulations, but there can be no assurance the Company’s employees, contractors or agents will not violate such laws and regulations or the Company’s policies and procedures. If the Company is found to have violated laws and regulations, it could materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations and financial condition. Regulatory changes and other actions that materially adversely affect the Company’s business may be announced with little or no advance notice and the Company may not be able to effectively mitigate all adverse impacts from such measures. For example, the Company is subject to changing regulations relating to the export and import of its products. Although the Company has programs, policies and procedures in place that are designed to satisfy regulatory requirements, there can be no assurance that such policies and procedures will be effective in preventing a violation or a claim of a violation. As a result, the Company’s products could be banned, delayed or prohibited from importation, which could materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations and financial condition.Expectations relating to environmental, social and governance considerations and related reporting obligations expose the Company to potential liabilities, increased costs, reputational harm, and other adverse effects on the Company’s business.Many governments, regulators, investors, employees, customers and other stakeholders are increasingly focused on environmental, social and governance considerations relating to businesses, including climate change and greenhouse gas emissions, human and civil rights, and diversity, equity and inclusion. In addition, the Company makes statements about its goals and initiatives through its various non-financial reports, information provided on its website, press statements and other communications. Responding to these environmental, social and governance considerations and implementation of these goals and initiatives involves risks and uncertainties, requires investments, and depends in part on third-party performance or data that is outside the Company’s control. The Company cannot guarantee that it will achieve its announced environmental, social and governance goals and initiatives. In addition, some stakeholders may disagree with the Company’s goals and initiatives.
